details:
**Les Fleurs du mal (The Flowers of Evil)**
Charles Baudelaire's 1857 poetry collection, the most common clue for French poetry. Its opening poem, "To the Reader," lists the sins that "occupy our minds," describes Ennui as a "refined monster" who "dreams of scaffolds" while smoking his hookah, and ends by addressing the "hypocrite reader, my likeness, my brother!" Its sections include "Spleen and Ideal" and "Wine."

**"The Albatross" and "The Swan"**
Two poems from Les Fleurs du mal. In "The Albatross," sailors capture the great bird, a "prince of the clouds" whose "great white wings" now drag beside him "like oars," and mock the "winged voyager" for how "comic and ugly" he is, an image of the poet among ordinary people. "The Swan" opens "Andromache, I think of you!" and mourns the old Paris torn down during the city's rebuilding.

**"The Drunken Boat" (Le Bateau ivre)**
Arthur Rimbaud's poem narrated by a boat drifting free after "yelping redskins" kill its haulers, nailing them "naked to colored stakes." Going "down impassive Rivers," the boat strikes "unbelievable Floridas," sees swamps "where a whole Leviathan rots in the rushes," and carries cargo of "Flemish wheat or English cotton."

**A Season in Hell (Une Saison en enfer)**
Rimbaud's long prose poem, which opens recalling a past "feast where all hearts opened and all wines flowed." Its sections include "Bad Blood" and two titled "Delirium"; the second, "Alchemy of the Word," begins with the speaker boasting that he "invented the color of vowels."

**"Vowels" (Voyelles)**
Rimbaud's sonnet assigning a color to each vowel: "A black, E white, I red, U green, O blue." Black A is a "hairy corset of shining flies" buzzing around foul smells.

**Négritude**
A literary movement of Black French-speaking writers who reclaimed African identity in response to colonialism. It was founded in 1930s Paris by its "three fathers": Aimé Césaire of Martinique, Léopold Sédar Senghor of Senegal, and Léon-Gontran Damas of French Guiana, whose collection Pigments was its first major volume. Jean-Paul Sartre's essay "Black Orpheus" introduced it to a wider audience, and Wole Soyinka mocked it by saying "a tiger does not proclaim its tigritude; it pounces."

**Notebook of a Return to My Native Land (Cahier d'un retour au pays natal)**
Aimé Césaire's long poem, a founding text of Négritude. It repeatedly begins sections with "At the end of daybreak..." to describe an inert, impoverished town in Martinique, opens by telling a "lousy pig" (or cop) to beat it, and coins new words such as "verrition."

**Léopold Sédar Senghor**
The Négritude poet who became the first president of Senegal. He wrote the collection Nocturnes and the poems "Black Woman" and "Prayer to Masks." In 1983 he became the first African elected to the Académie française, the official body that regulates the French language.

**Césaire's A Tempest (Une Tempête)**
Aimé Césaire's anti-colonial adaptation of Shakespeare's The Tempest. Caliban is recast as a rebellious Black slave who rejects the name Prospero gave him and demands to be called "X."

**Eugène Ionesco**
A Romanian-born playwright of the Theater of the Absurd who wrote in French. In The Bald Soprano, the Smiths and the Martins have absurd conversations, including about a family full of people named Bobby Watson; the Martins discover they share a daughter named Alice with one red eye; and the Fire Chief tells fables and notes that the bald soprano "always wears her hair the same way." In The Chairs, an old couple jump out of a window before an Orator writes nonsense like "ANGELFOOD" on a blackboard, and in Rhinoceros, Bérenger alone resists turning into a rhinoceros.

**Molière**
A playwright at the court of Louis XIV. In Tartuffe, the religious hypocrite of the title tries to seduce Elmire while her husband Orgon hides under a table; Tartuffe then claims Orgon's house and uses a box of incriminating papers belonging to Orgon's friend Argas. In The Imaginary Invalid, the hypochondriac Argan tries to marry his daughter to Thomas Diafoirus, the nephew of his doctor Purgon.

**Oulipo and Georges Perec**
Oulipo is a French group of writers who use constrained writing. Its member Georges Perec wrote A Void (La Disparition), a novel without the letter "e," and Life: A User's Manual, which moves through every apartment of a Paris building following a chess knight's tour. In it, the wealthy Bartlebooth paints seascapes, has Gaspard Winckler turn them into jigsaw puzzles, and then solves them.

**French novels: Proust, Camus, Gide, and Céline**
Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time opens "For a long time, I went to bed early" and recalls the narrator's childhood magic lantern and his wait for his mother's goodnight kiss. Its most famous moment is the tea-soaked madeleine that brings back his memories. Other French clues include Albert Camus's The Stranger ("Maman died today") and The Plague, set in Oran with Dr. Bernard Rieux; André Gide's The Immoralist, about Michel's honeymoon in Tunisia; and Louis-Ferdinand Céline's Journey to the End of the Night, about Bardamu's adventures in Africa and America.

**Other French poets: Verlaine, Valéry, and Apollinaire**
Paul Verlaine wrote "Autumn Song," whose long sobs of the violins wound the heart, and "Moonlight," which begins "Your soul is a chosen landscape." Paul Valéry's "The Graveyard by the Sea" contains "The wind is rising!... We must try to live!", which gave Hayao Miyazaki's film The Wind Rises its title. Guillaume Apollinaire's "Zone" ends with the phrase "sun slit throat."

**Jules Verne, Cyrano, and Québécois French**
Jules Verne's Extraordinary Voyages include Journey to the Center of the Earth, in which a German professor decodes a runic message and travels underground with his nephew, past dinosaurs and giant mushrooms, until they come out at Stromboli, and From the Earth to the Moon, about the Baltimore Gun Club's giant cannon. Earlier, Cyrano de Bergerac wrote satirical "Comical Histories" of the states and empires of the moon and sun, and Voltaire wrote Micromégas. In Quebec, Michel Tremblay's play Les Belles-Sœurs (The Sisters-in-Law) brought the working-class joual dialect to the stage.
